summary: King of León from 999 to 1028 who came to the throne at five, rebuilt a capital that Almanzor had burned, gave the kingdom its first written law in the Fuero de León of 1017, and was killed by an arrow while besieging Viseu.
details: Alfonso V ruled through a regency until 1008 and then spent twenty years repairing the damage of the Andalusi raids: resettling León, restoring its churches, and summoning a council that issued both a code for the kingdom and a charter of liberties for the city. He died on campaign in 1028, leaving an eleven-year-old heir and a realm about to pass by marriage to the Navarrese.

greatestFeats: Issued the Fuero de León in 1017, the first written law of the kingdom

birth.note: Son of Bermudo II of León and his second wife Elvira García, daughter of the count of Castile; he was about five when his father died.

death.circumstance: Struck by an arrow while reconnoitring the walls during the siege of Viseu, in the Muslim-held country south of the Douro. His body was carried back to León and buried in the church of San Juan Bautista, later rebuilt as the basilica of San Isidoro.

The miniature was painted about ninety years after the king’s death and shows the office rather than the man. Public domain.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Alfonso V was king of León from 999 to 1028. He inherited at about five years old, in the worst decade the kingdom had known: Almanzor had sacked León itself in 988 and Santiago de Compostela in 997, and the monarchy survived on the strength of its mountains and its charters rather than its armies. His mother Elvira García and Count Menendo González governed for him until 1008.

What he is remembered for is not war but law and reconstruction. He rebuilt León with earth and brick where stone had been thrown down, repopulated it, and in 1017 held a full curia in the cathedral that issued the Fuero de León — a set of decrees for the whole kingdom together with a charter of liberties for the city and its district, the earliest such compilation in the peninsula. He was killed by an arrow in 1028 while besieging Viseu, aged about thirty-four.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born about 994 to Bermudo II of León and Elvira García, a daughter of the Castilian comital house. His father died in 999 after a reign spent absorbing Almanzor’s campaigns, and the crown passed to a child of five. The regency was held jointly by his mother and by Count Menendo González of Galicia, who took the boy into his own household in Galicia and raised him there; Alfonso later married Menendo’s daughter, which says plainly enough where the power in the minority lay.

He began to rule for himself on Menendo’s death in 1008. The kingdom he took over had lost its capital to fire twenty years earlier and much of its southern settlement to raiding, but the danger was already receding: Almanzor had died in 1002 and the caliphate of Córdoba was sliding towards the collapse that came in 1031. Alfonso’s reign falls almost exactly into that gap, which is why a king of León could spend it on building rather than on defence.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: The man is unusually hard to see behind his own government, and the reason is the shape of the evidence. Sampiro, the court notary who became Alfonso’s majordomo and then bishop of Astorga, wrote the chronicle that covers the previous century and a half — but it stops around 982, before this reign, so the one writer who actually knew Alfonso V did not describe him. What survives instead is institutional: charters, the acts of the curia of 1017, and the record of what was rebuilt.

Later chroniclers filled the gap with approval. The Historia silense, written at León in the early twelfth century, and Pelayo of Oviedo’s recension after it praise him as a restorer of churches and laws; Lucas de Tuy, assembling the Chronicon mundi at San Isidoro in 1236, inherited that view and passed it on to Castilian tradition, where he became Alfonso the Noble. Every one of those writers belonged to a Leonese church that had been endowed or rebuilt by him or in his name, which is a reason to trust their facts about buildings and to discount their adjectives about the builder.

What can be said with confidence comes from the acts themselves. The decrees of 1017 regulate inheritance, the conduct of royal officers, sanctuary, and the obligations of the men of León in terms that assume a ruined city needing settlers and guarantees rather than a triumphant one needing discipline. A king who legislates about who may take a vacant house, and on what terms a newcomer keeps it, is a king solving the problem in front of him. He also died leading a siege at thirty-four, which is not the death of a purely clerical prince.

contentSections.title: A kingdom to rebuild
paragraphs: The destruction of 988 was not symbolic. Almanzor’s troops broke the walls and burned the churches of León, and the Andalusi raids of the following decade reached Santiago de Compostela itself in 997, carrying off the cathedral bells. The monarchy did not fall, because the raids were plunder rather than conquest and left no garrisons behind, but the capital was a ruin and the Duero settlements were thinned.

Alfonso’s response was to rebuild cheaply and quickly and to attract people back. The walls went up again, the churches were repaired, and the fuero gave incoming settlers terms worth accepting — the same frontier bargain of land and liberties for defence that the Leonese crown used everywhere on its southern edge. He also restored the church of San Juan Bautista beside the palace, where his father was buried and where he would be buried himself; rebuilt in stone later in the century, it became the basilica of San Isidoro and the royal pantheon of León.

contentSections.title: The Fuero de León
paragraphs: On 30 July 1017 Alfonso held a plena curia — the bishops, abbots and magnates of the whole realm — in the cathedral of León, and it issued what is known as the Fuero de León. It is in two parts: about twenty decrees binding on the entire kingdom, covering the church, royal officials, inheritance and the protection of persons, and a further twenty-eight precepts applying specifically to the city of León and its surrounding district, fixing the rights and duties of its inhabitants, the conduct of its market and the terms on which settlers held their property.

The date has been argued over for a century, and the argument is worth stating plainly rather than hiding. Until the early twentieth century 1020 was the accepted year, and Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz defended it from the copy preserved in the Liber testamentorum of Oviedo; Ramón Menéndez Pidal argued for 1017; and in 1992 Gonzalo Martínez Díez concluded for 1017 on the ground that the copy surviving at Braga is earlier than the Oviedo one. A further view holds that both are right in part — that the decrees for the kingdom came from the curia of 1017 and the municipal precepts for the city were added around 1020. The text as it stands is a compilation, and that is the most likely reason the dates disagree.

Its importance is that it is first. Before 1017 Leonese law was custom plus the Visigothic Liber Iudiciorum; after it, a Christian Iberian kingdom had a written statement of what the king owed his subjects and what they owed him, and a city had a charter it could cite against royal officers. Every later Leonese and Castilian fuero, down to the charters of the Extremaduran towns two centuries afterwards, works in the form Alfonso’s curia set.

contentSections.title: Marriages and the Navarrese shadow
paragraphs: In 1013 Alfonso married Elvira Menéndez, the daughter of the count who had raised him. She bore his heir Bermudo III and a daughter, Sancha, and died on 2 December 1022. In 1023 he married again, to Urraca Garcés of the Navarrese royal house, sister of Sancho III the Great of Pamplona.

That second marriage points at the direction power was moving. Sancho III was building a hegemony across the whole Christian north, and within a decade of Alfonso’s death he was intervening directly in León and detaching Castile from it. The consequences fell on Alfonso’s children: his son Bermudo III was killed at Tamarón in 1037 fighting Sancho’s son Fernando, who had married Alfonso’s daughter Sancha and who took the Leonese crown by right of his wife. The Asturian line that had ruled since Pelayo ended with Alfonso’s son, and the kingdom passed to the Navarrese dynasty.

contentSections.title: Death at Viseu
paragraphs: With Córdoba disintegrating, Alfonso went on the offensive in the west, down the old Roman road towards the Mondego and the Douro country. In the summer of 1028 he was besieging the Muslim-held town of Viseu. On Wednesday 7 August, while he was examining the walls, an arrow struck him and killed him.

He was about thirty-four and had reigned for twenty-nine years. His body was taken back to León and buried in the church of San Juan Bautista, the royal pantheon he had restored. His heir Bermudo III was eleven years old, and the guardianship fell to the widowed Queen Urraca Garcés — a minority following a minority, in a kingdom whose most dangerous neighbour was now Christian and related by marriage.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Alfonso V is the king who made León a working capital rather than a burnt one, and the Fuero is the reason his name survived. A millennium later the city kept its anniversary: 1017 to 2017 was marked in León as the thousand years of the fuero, and the document is the foundation of the claim that the Leonese crown wrote European law early. The claim can be overstated — the fuero is a compilation whose parts may be three years apart, and the kingdom-wide decrees are thinner than the municipal ones — but the substance holds, that a king in 1017 put in writing the liberties of a town and the limits on his own officers.

The second legacy is the pantheon. By restoring San Juan Bautista as the burial church of the dynasty he gave the Leonese monarchy a place to bury its dead in the capital, and his descendants used it: the Romanesque chamber built over it holds the kings and queens of León down to the twelfth century, including Queen Urraca, who chose it against her own father’s example. The kingdom Alfonso rebuilt lasted two hundred years after him and ended, under Alfonso IX, still ruled from the city he had put back on its feet.

keyAchievements.title: The Fuero de León, 1017
keyAchievements.description: A plena curia in León cathedral issued decrees for the whole kingdom and a charter of liberties for the city — the first such compilation in Christian Iberia.

keyAchievements.title: The capital rebuilt
keyAchievements.description: Restored the walls, churches and population of León after Almanzor burned it in 988, using settlement terms to draw people back.

keyAchievements.title: The royal pantheon restored
keyAchievements.description: Rebuilt San Juan Bautista beside the palace as the dynasty’s burial church; it became the basilica of San Isidoro.

keyAchievements.title: A minority survived
keyAchievements.description: Held the throne through nine years of regency under his mother Elvira García and Count Menendo González, and ruled alone from 1008.

timeline.title: King at five
timeline.description: Succeeds his father Bermudo II under the joint regency of his mother Elvira García and Count Menendo González, who raises him in Galicia.

timeline.title: Rules in his own right
timeline.description: Menendo González dies and the young king takes the government of the realm himself.

timeline.title: Marries Elvira Menéndez
timeline.description: Weds the daughter of his late guardian; their children are the heir Bermudo III and Sancha, who would carry León to the Navarrese line.

timeline.title: The Fuero de León
timeline.description: A full curia in the cathedral issues decrees for the kingdom and a charter of liberties for the city and its district.

timeline.title: Marries Urraca Garcés
timeline.description: Takes a sister of Sancho III the Great of Pamplona, as Navarrese power begins to close around the Leonese kingdom.

timeline.title: Killed at Viseu
timeline.description: Struck by an arrow during the siege of the Muslim-held town; his body is returned to León and his eleven-year-old son succeeds.

predecessor.note: His father, who reigned from 984 to 999 and absorbed the worst of Almanzor’s campaigns, leaving a five-year-old heir and a burnt capital.

successor.note: His son, eleven at his accession and the last king of the Asturian line in León; killed at Tamarón in 1037, after which the crown passed to his sister’s husband Fernando I.
